analysis.one_liner: Lets families and police ask a federal court to temporarily remove guns from people in crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 114 House Democrats and no Republicans, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since February 17, 2026, with no action and no scheduled vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a federal 'red flag' process: a family member or police officer can ask a federal court to bar a person who is an imminent danger to themselves or others from buying or keeping guns for up to 180 days. A judge must find probable cause for a temporary 14-day order, then hold a hearing with notice, a lawyer for the person if they can't afford one, and a 'clear and convincing' standard of proof before a longer order lasts. Guns are surrendered to federal marshals and returned if the order expires, and the bill funds state and tribal governments to run their own similar programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People in crisis and the people around them — family members worried about a suicide risk or a domestic abuser with guns, and communities affected by gun violence. The bill also explicitly lets respondents sell surrendered guns to licensed dealers and requires courts to return them once an order lapses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Allows a family or household member or a law enforcement officer to petition a federal court to temporarily bar a person posing a risk of imminent injury to themselves or others from purchasing or possessing firearms.

Requires a sworn affidavit and a probable-cause finding for an emergency 14-day order, then a hearing within 72 hours with notice, a right to counsel (court-provided if the person cannot afford one), and clear-and-convincing evidence for an order lasting at most 180 days.
Prohibits any fees for filing or responding to a petition and penalizes knowingly false or frivolous petitions with fines up to $5,000 or up to 5 years in prison.

Adds people subject to these orders to the federal list of those prohibited from receiving or possessing firearms and requires the FBI to collect records identifying them so background checks catch them.

Creates a Justice Department grant program for states, local governments, and Indian tribes that enact similar laws, with at least 25% of grant money reserved for law enforcement training that covers bias, domestic violence safety planning, and de-escalation.
Requires surrendered firearms to be returned if an order expires or is dissolved and the person is otherwise legally allowed to own them.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm owners named in petitions lose temporary possession of their guns and any concealed-carry permit while an order is in effect, even before the full hearing. The Justice Department, courts, and U.S. Marshals Service take on new duties funded by unspecified appropriations, and licensed gun dealers become the optional channel for selling surrendered firearms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners named in petitions, and federal agencies

drawbacks.text: A person can lose their firearms under an ex parte order they had no chance to contest, based on a one-sided affidavit and a probable-cause finding; the safeguard is that the order lasts only 14 days unless a contested hearing upholds it.

The grant program is conditioned on states enacting laws 'substantially similar' to federal requirements, which critics of federal red flag schemes argue pressures states to adopt a one-size-fits-all process regardless of local law.

Petitions can be filed by family members without legal training, raising the possibility of disputes being litigated through gun removal; the bill responds with a penalty for frivolous or false petitions but a wrongly named person still loses their guns temporarily.
The bill authorizes spending 'such sums as are necessary' without a funding source, leaving the cost of grants, court hearings, and marshal services open-ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed with more due-process protection than most state red flag laws — probable cause for emergency orders, a 72-hour hearing, court-appointed counsel, clear-and-convincing proof for anything longer, and criminal penalties for abuse. The core trade-off is unavoidable: someone can be disarmed for up to 14 days before getting their day in court, which is the point of an emergency order but a real civil-liberties cost. The grant program's open-ended funding and its pressure on states to conform are the weakest parts of the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the Federal Extreme Risk Protection Order Act of 2026 on February 17, 2026, with 113 original cosponsors.
All 113 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the public action history shows no further steps.
With Republicans holding 223 of 435 House seats, a bill with no Republican cosponsors cannot reach 218 votes on the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's conduct has changed: gun owners face no new federal restrictions, and the firearms industry faces no new federal requirements, while people at risk of gun violence remain without a federal red flag remedy. The decisive fact is that the House majority has not acted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the gun industry

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on February 17, 2026.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Republican-led)
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair has taken no action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 17, 2026, and has held no hearing or markup; no vote has been scheduled.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No member has cosponsored the bill, and the majority has not scheduled floor action.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposes federal red flag legislation as a category and has campaigned against similar bills in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 114 of 217 House Democrats signed on as sponsor or cosponsor — while none of the 223 House Republicans has, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee has taken no action.

industries.note: A federal red flag process would remove some would-be customers from the market — people subject to orders are barred from buying or possessing guns. But the bill also lets respondents sell surrendered firearms to federally licensed dealers, and the industry has generally opposed red flag laws as a category. [S3]
When a person under an order chooses to sell rather than surrender their guns, the bill directs those sales to a federally licensed dealer, routing firearms removal through dealers. [S3]

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement and courts
industries.note: Grant money would fund personnel, training, court protocols, and data collection for states, local governments, and tribes that adopt similar laws, with at least 25% reserved for officer training. [S3]

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing, no markup, no Republican support, and a Republican-held House, the practical path is that the bill sits in the Judiciary Committee until this Congress ends in January 2027, as most gun-related bills without majority-party sponsorship do. It is likely to be reintroduced in a future Congress.
